{{Short description|Genus of theropod dinosaur}} {{Speciesbox | fossil_range = [[Late Cretaceous]]
(mid-[[Campanian]]), ~{{fossilrange|76.72|76.35}} {{period fossil range|Cretaceous|76.72|76.35}} | image = Daspletosaur.jpg | image_caption = Skull of the [[holotype specimen]] | display_parents = 2 | genus = Tromerosaurus | parent_authority = Powers et al., [[2026 in archosaur paleontology|2026]] | species = solumons | authority = Powers et al., 2026 }} '''''Tromerosaurus''''' ({{lit|terrible lizard}}) is an [[extinct]] genus of [[tyrannosaurid]] theropod dinosaur known from the [[Late Cretaceous]] ([[Campanian]] age) of Canada. The genus contains a [[Monotypic taxon|single species]], '''''Tromerosaurus solumons''''', known from at least three partial skulls and skeletons. Previous work had regarded one of these, deriving from the [[Oldman Formation]], as belonging to ''[[Daspletosaurus]]'', and two of them, from the [[Dinosaur Park Formation]], as belonging to the closely related ''[[Gorgosaurus]]''. A placement within the subfamily [[Albertosaurinae]] is preferred, though some anatomical features of ''Tromerosaurus'' are reminiscent of [[tyrannosaurine]]s. == Discovery and naming == [[File:Mybones.jpg|thumb|left|Excavation of the holotype in 2010]] In 2010, Stuart Plotkin discovered the remains of a tyrannosaur skeleton in outcrops of the upper [[Oldman Formation]] (quarry Q258) in eastern [[Dinosaur Provincial Park]] in [[Alberta]], Canada. A team from the [[University of Alberta]] (UA) assisted in [[Fossil collection|excavating]] the specimen in 2010 and 2011. The specimen is now housed in the UA Laboratory for Vertebrate Paleontology (UALVP), where it is [[Accession number (cultural property)|accessioned]] as specimen UALVP 52981. It consists of a partially articulated, albeit incomplete, skeleton including most of the skull (missing the {{dinogloss|splenials}} and some components of the right half) and much of the [[postcranium]] (vertebrae from the neck and trunk, {{dinogloss|gastralia}}, ribs, both {{dinogloss|humeri}}, the {{dinogloss|pelvis}}, and most of the right hindlimb). Initial reports in the early 2020s identified this specimen as belonging to ''[[Daspletosaurus]]'' without discussion. The discovery of this specimen prompted the reanalysis of two partial skeletons from the lower rock layers of the [[Dinosaur Park Formation]], which overlies the Oldman Formation. Both of these specimens, housed in the [[Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology]] (TMP), had been previously mentioned in the scientific literature as belonging to the closely related genus ''[[Gorgosaurus]]''. TMP 1994.012.0602, which includes much of the skull and tail, in addition to gastralia, ribs, most of both hindlimbs, and the pelvis, has been regarded as the largest and most mature adult specimen of ''G. libratus''. TMP 1995.005.0001, a smaller partial skeleton, comprises an incomplete, disarticulated skull and an [[Fossil preparation|unprepared]] pelvis. [[File:Daspletosaur pelvis.jpg|thumb|left|alt=|[[Pelvis]] of the holotype on exhibit]] In 2026, Mark J. Powers and colleagues [[Species description|described]] ''Tromerosaurus solumons'' as a new genus and species of tyrannosaurid theropod based on these fossil remains, designating UALVP 52981 as the [[holotype]] specimen. TMP 1994.012.0602 and TMP 1995.005.0001 were referred to this species based on shared anatomical features with the holotype. Two isolated {{dinogloss|maxillae}} (primary upper tooth-bearing bones) from unknown localities were tentatively also referred, one of which (UALVP 56605) belongs to a mature individual, while the other (TMP 1985.011.0003) belongs to a small juvenile. This smaller bone was first assigned to ''[[Albertosaurus libratus]]'' in 1999. === Etymology === [[File:Daspletosaur limb.jpg|thumb|right|alt=|Leg of the holotype]] The [[Genus|generic name]], ''Tromerosaurus'', is combines the [[Ancient Greek]] words {{lang|grc|[[:wikt:τρομερός|τρομερός]]}} ({{lang|grc|tromerós}}), meaning {{gloss|terrible}} or {{gloss|frightful}}, and {{lang|grc|[[wikt:σαῦρος#Etymology|σαῦρος]]}} ({{lang|grc|saûros}}), meaning {{gloss|lizard}}. This alludes to the combination of anatomical traits it shares with ''Gorgosaurus'' ({{lit|terrible lizard}}) and ''Daspletosaurus'' ({{lit|frightful lizard}}). The [[Specific name (zoology)|specific name]], ''solumons'', is derived from the [[Latin]] words {{lang|la|[[:wikt:solus|solus]]}}, meaning {{gloss|lonely}}, and {{lang|la|[[:wikt:mons#Latin|mōns]]}}, meaning {{gloss|mountain}}. This references the anatomy of the {{dinogloss|lacrimal}} horn, which is isolated by a wide, flattened shelf of the bone's posterior process. It also alludes to the dragon [[Smaug]] and his lair on [[Lonely Mountain]] in [[J. R. R. Tolkien|J. R. R. Tolkien's]] 1937 fantasy novel ''[[The Hobbit]]'', hinting at the visual parallels between [[dragon]] iconography and tyrannosaurids. == Description == [[File:Tromerosaurus Size Comparison.svg|thumb|Size of two ''Tromerosaurus'' specimens compared to a human]] As preserved, ''T. solumons'' holotype skull is disarticulated, with the components no longer in their natural anatomical placements. When digitally reconstructed, its greatest length is {{convert|.9|m|ft}}. The {{dinogloss|femur}} is longer, at {{cvt|.95|m|ft}}. This condition, with a skull shorter than the femur, is more similar to albertosaurine tyrannosaurids than tyrannosaurines, in which the skull is generally longer. The snout comprises more than 60% of the skull's length, and the skull maintains a broadly consistent depth from the snout to the back of the cranium. The braincase of the holotype is [[taphonomically]] compressed, but the braincase of one of the referred specimens indicates the [[Temporal fenestra|temporal region]] is [[Anatomical terms of location#Medial and lateral|laterally]] wide, a feature shared by tyrannosaurines and ''[[Nanotyrannus]]''. The maxillae of the ''T. solumons'' holotype bear 13 teeth, in contrast to the 15 teeth in the referred specimen TMP 1994.012.0602. Most specimens of ''Albertosaurus'', ''Gorgosaurus'', and ''[[Teratophoneus]]'' have 14 maxillary teeth, and the standard maxillary tooth count variation in tyrannosaurids is ±1. The {{dinogloss|dentary}} has 16 teeth, within the range of 15–18 seen in ''Gorgosaurus''. == Classification == [[File:Tromerosaurus solumons life reconstruction.png|thumb|[[Life restoration]] of ''Tromerosaurus'']] To test the affinities and relationships of ''Tromerosaurus'', Powers et al. (2026) included it in an updated version of the [[phylogenetic]] matrix of Voris (2025). In all versions of their [[Maximum parsimony|parsimony analyses]], ''Tromerosaurus'' was recovered as the [[Basal (phylogenetics)|basalmost]] member of the [[tyrannosaurid]] subfamily [[Albertosaurinae]], which also includes ''[[Albertosaurus]]'' and ''[[Gorgosaurus]]''. These results are displayed in '''Topology A''' below. This is comparable to the parsimony and [[Bayesian inference in phylogeny|Bayesian]] results recovered the year prior using an independent dataset developed and published by Zanno and Napoli. These researchers recovered the ''T. solumons'' holotype (then unnamed) as the [[sister taxon]] to ''Gorgosaurus'' + ''Albertosaurus'', though the exact composition of earlier-diverging albertosaurines varied between methods.
